name: Psychedelic therapy for self-image

lead: Psychedelic therapy is the use of drugs such as psilocybin, LSD and MDMA, with preparation and integration sessions, in mental health treatment. Some forum users float it as a way to reshape how they see their own appearance and gain self-acceptance and confidence.

The chain: guided psychedelic sessions, a shifted view of self-image, more self-acceptance. Research has focused on depression, PTSD, anxiety and substance use. The only body-image item is a 2024 review in which a single psilocybin dose given for OCD symptoms raised insight in patients who also had body dysmorphic disorder, leading them to seek treatment.

paras: Clinical use is in supervised sessions with preparation beforehand and integration afterward, generally within clinical trials. Outcomes are described as depending heavily on mindset and setting, and mechanisms are poorly understood.
The drugs are Schedule I in the US. Contraindications include psychosis history, pregnancy and SSRI use, and some medications and psychiatric histories rule it out.

angle.text: Some forum users float psilocybin, LSD or MDMA therapy as a way to reshape how they see their own appearance and reach more self-acceptance. Research has focused on depression, PTSD and anxiety, and no direct body-image studies exist.

lead: Psychedelic therapy for self-image is the idea that psychedelic-assisted treatment with substances such as psilocybin, LSD or MDMA could change how a person perceives and feels about their own body and appearance. Interest comes from people with appearance-related distress, including body dysmorphic disorder (BDD), who seek a shift in self-perception so they can feel at ease with how they look rather than changing their looks themselves.[1][2]

Psychedelic therapy more broadly is the use of these drugs in mental health treatment, usually with preparation and integration sessions, and research has concentrated on depression, PTSD, anxiety and substance use.[1] Wikipedia describes psilocybin at high doses as producing ego dissolution, with decreased connectivity in the default mode network, a system tied to introspection and sense of self.[3] A 2024 review noted that a single psilocybin dose given for obsessive-compulsive symptoms raised insight in patients who also had BDD, leading them to seek treatment.[1]

A PubMed search for psilocybin and BDD lists a small body of work, including a 2023 pilot study of single-dose psilocybin in serotonin-reuptake-inhibitor-resistant BDD, a 2025 study of resting-state brain networks after a single dose in BDD patients, a 1996 case report, and a 2020 review of psychedelics and the aberrant bodily self.[4] Psychedelics remain Schedule I in the US and are generally limited to clinical trials.
infobox: Schedule I (US); trials or limited programs elsewhere[3]

paras: Wikipedia describes BDD as involving extreme misperceptions of one's appearance, commonly of the face, skin or body, with a muscle dysmorphia subtype in which people see their bodies as too small. Established treatments are SSRIs and cognitive-behavioural therapy, and it notes that cosmetic surgery often does not relieve BDD symptoms.[5]

A 2024 meta-analysis of psilocybin trials found antidepressant effects above placebo, and an FDA panel in 2024 voted against approving MDMA for PTSD.[1] Limitations include small samples, short follow-up and blinding problems.[1] Wikipedia notes psilocybin was approved in Australia for treatment-resistant depression in 2023 and that single doses with psychological support may produce rapid antidepressant effects, with an advantage over continuous SSRI use that may be modest or absent.[3]
For BDD specifically, three published items were identified in PubMed: a 1996 case report by Hanes on serotonin, psilocybin and BDD, a 2023 pilot study, and a 2025 imaging study.[4][6][7][8]

The 2023 pilot study by Schneier, Feusner, Wheaton and colleagues was an open-label trial with no control group, in 12 adults (8 women, 4 men) with moderate-to-severe nondelusional BDD that had not responded to at least one serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Each received a single oral psilocybin dose with psychological support. BDD-YBOCS symptom scores fell significantly over 12 weeks with a large effect size, secondary measures of belief conviction, negative affect and disability also improved, no serious adverse events occurred, and seven participants (58 percent) were responders at week 12, defined as at least a 30 percent score reduction. The authors described the findings as preliminary support that warrants controlled studies.[6][9]

The 2025 imaging study by Zhu, Hellerstein and colleagues enrolled eight adults with moderate-to-severe nondelusional BDD, gave one oral psilocybin dose with psychological support and used resting-state fMRI the day before and day after dosing. It was uncontrolled. Symptom scores fell at weeks 1 and 12, connectivity within the executive control network increased on day one, and increases within that network and between it and the default mode and salience networks predicted improvement at week 1. The authors called for larger controlled studies.[7][9]

A 2020 review by Ho, Preller and Lenggenhager examined neuropharmacological modulation of the aberrant bodily self through psychedelics, noting that several psychiatric disorders involve aberrant perceptions of the bodily self.[10]

Wikipedia describes high-dose psilocybin as producing ego dissolution with decreased default mode network connectivity, a network tied to introspection and sense of self.[3] The 2025 imaging study found that changes in executive control, default mode and salience network connectivity were related to symptom change in BDD, though the sample was small and had no comparison group.[7]

Psychedelic therapy attracted wide media and investor attention in the 2020s. In 2024 an FDA advisory panel voted against approving MDMA for PTSD, while Australia approved psilocybin for treatment-resistant depression in 2023.[1][3] In looks-focused communities, interest takes the form of questions about whether such drugs could reduce appearance anxiety; the published work so far is confined to supervised BDD studies, and the drugs are Schedule I in the US.[3]

Contraindications include pregnancy, serious cardiovascular disease, SSRI or MAOI use, and a personal or family history of psychosis or bipolar I disorder.[1] Wikipedia lists panic reactions as common, hallucinogen-induced psychotic disorder as rare (under 1 percent of users), and notes psilocybin is Schedule I under the 1971 UN Convention, with possession of psilocybin mushrooms illegal in most countries.[3]

Small studies in body dysmorphic disorder exist: a 2023 open-label pilot of 12 adults, a 2025 uncontrolled imaging study of 8 adults and a 1996 case report; no controlled trial and no studies of psychedelics for everyday looks-related self-image outside that diagnosis were found.[4][6][7][8] A 2024 review noted increased insight in OCD patients with body dysmorphic disorder after psilocybin.[1]

timeline.event: Hanes publishes a case report on serotonin, psilocybin and body dysmorphic disorder.[8]
